title: Vetting Signals and Synthesis: GTM Notes for Model Catalog
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note for the GTM & product teams to converge on a practical, defensible set of signals and an evidence synthesis approach for the Model Catalog. Goal: produce a lightweight ‘verified profiles’ concept that sales and docs can use, while preserving engineering-friendly verifiability and avoiding overclaiming on model properties.

Scope / Context:
- Focus: open models and community variants we plan to list in the catalog.
- Why now: rising customer questions about model reliability, hallucination risk, and which open models are good for production. We need repeatable, channel-ready messaging that maps to observable signals engineers can validate.
- Constraints: limited compute budget for re-running expensive evals; cannot run exhaustive safety assays for every model.

Audience & use cases:
- Sales/AE: quick one-line signals to qualify fit and handle objections.
- Developer / ML engineers: reproducible checks they can run or inspect.
- Solutions architects: deeper notes for architecture choices and fallback policies.

High-level GTM proposition (working):
- "Verified Profiles" (working name): a concise, three-part snapshot per model: Primary Capabilities, Empirical Reliability, Operational Footprint.
- Claims are backed by incremental evidence tiers (self-reported, Redwood-run quick checks, Redwood-verified results).

Signal taxonomy (candidate list — prioritize cheap & high-leverage):
1) Functional performance (accuracy/coverage)
   - Small benchmark suites (domain-specific unit prompts, 50–200 examples).
   - Win/Loss ratio versus baseline (e.g., Redbench-lite).
2) Hallucination / factuality proxy
   - Fact-lookup stability: percent of answers that match web-searched snippets (automated weak-signal).
   - Named-entity hallucination rate on templated prompts.
3) Safety & toxicity surface
   - Off-the-shelf toxicity classifier pass rate (toxicity models are proxies).
   - Known red-team hits (sourced from community reports).
4) Latency & inference cost
   - p50/p95 gen latency at 1k token budget on standard infra profile (our standard config).
   - Relative token cost delta vs curated baseline.
5) Determinism / sampling character
   - Variance across seeds for fixed prompts (stability score).
6) Provenance & lineage
   - Model checkpoint origin (OSS repo, weights provenance statements).
   - Licensing constraints and redistributability.
7) Robustness to instruction tuning
   - Sensitive metrics: instruction-following score on small checklist.

Evidence tiers (practical, not absolute):
- Tier 0: Vendor / repo claims and README notes (self-reported).
- Tier 1: Redwood quick-checks — low-cost automated probes we run across our standard harness (fast, reproducible).
- Tier 2: Redwood curated evals — larger eval suites, spot-checks across domains, and optional safety scans.
- Tier 3: Deep validation — customer-funded or partner projects with targeted benchmark suites and traceable prompts.

How to compose a profile (proposed short template for sales docs):
- One-line elevator: capability summary + best-fit workloads.
- Quick metric strip: (Tier level badge), p50/p95 latency, hallucination proxy %, instruction-follow F1.
- Top 3 caveats / known issues.
- Recommended production setup: quantization suggestions, batching guidance, cache/prefix tips.
- Links: model repo, license, Redwood quick-check report (pdf/mini-report).

Competitive analysis (notes / differentiating angles):
- OpenAI / Anthropic: strong brand + curated endpoints; they own trust but are less flexible on open-weight variants. They win when buyers prioritize brand-trust and consistency.
- Hugging Face: discovery + community signals (stars, downloads), but quality varies and discovery noise is high. HF is a place customers will check; we should complement HF by surfacing operational signals (latency, p50, quantization friendliness).
- Replicate / third-party runtimes: convenience vs. variable infra performance. We should emphasize Redwood’s inference-first metrics (latency SLOs, batching behavior) as a differential.
- Self-hosting (customers building own stacks): cost tradeoffs and engineering overhead. Position Redwood for teams that want control without full ops build.

Messaging levers & sample lines:
- For engineers: "See the short, reproducible quick-check we ran — run it yourself or use our harness. You’ll know what fails on your prompts in <30m."
- For product leaders: "Verified Profiles surface the real operational cost and failure modes so you can budget and set rollback plans before rollout."
- For security/compliance buyers: "Profiles include provenance and license flags and explicit guidance for private deployments and KMS integration."

Sales objections & suggested responses (working):
- "How do we trust Redwood's tests?" -> "We publish the quick-check harness and test prompts; reproducibility is core — run the same probes in your environment or ask for a runbook."
- "Is this a guarantee of performance?" -> "No — profiles are evidence snapshots. We recommend a short pilot to validate for your prompt distribution; our tooling measures regression ties to prompts."
- "Why not just use HF metrics?" -> "HF shows popularity but not operational latency, hallucination proxies, or our reproducible quick-checks tailored for inference economics."

Evidence collection plan (practical sequence):
1) Build 10–15 lightweight quick-checks (cross-domain): search QA, summarization, instruction-follow, coding, classification. Reuse existing Redwood harness tests where possible. (Owner: Ethan)
2) Run Tier 1 scans on top 40 candidate open models we intend to surface. (Owner: Sasha)
3) Triage high-variance models for Tier 2 runs (where Tier1 indicates instability or surprising strengths). (Owner: Priya)
4) Draft profile template and sample 5 profiles for marketing & sales review. (Owner: Priya + Luca)

Metrics to watch (for GTM success):
- Time-to-first-validation: median minutes for a customer to run a quick-check in their environment.
- Number of profiles adopted in sales collateral in 60 days.
- Reduction in "model quality" related RFP questions after profiles roll out.
- Pilot-to-paid conversion for customers using profiles in evaluation.

Open questions / risks:
- How to surface uncertainty succinctly? (single badge vs multiple fields)
- If customers misinterpret Tier 1 as full validation, we risk overpromising. Need clear disclaimers.
- Compute cost: Tier 2 runs are expensive. Propose a payment model for deep validation (customer-funded) or partner-funded validation.

Proposed next steps (immediate):
- Align with Product: confirm standard infra profile for latency/cost measures (ticket: JIRA:GTMS-614). (Due: 2026-02-20)
- Produce the first 5 Tier 1 quick-check reports and share with Sales for feedback. (Due: 2026-03-05)
- Draft a single-page "profile" layout and test in one-sheeter for AE use. (Due: 2026-03-12)
- Schedule cross-functional review: GTM, Product, Applied ML, SRE. (Owner: Priya)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: prioritize reproducibility and low-friction evidence.
- We can iterate on badges and UI once the underlying signals prove useful in sales cycles.
- Please flag any legal/licensing redlines if we surface certain models; we should loop in legal early for models with ambiguous licenses.

Appendix: quick sample mini-profile (text mockup)
- Name: example-open-7b-v2
- Elevator: affordable instruction-tuned 7B for short-form summarization and chat-like flows; good for internal tooling and lightweight assistants.
- Tier: Tier 1 (Redwood quick-check)
- Key numbers: p50=110ms, p95=420ms (standard infra), hallucination proxy=12%, instruction-follow F1=0.78
- Caveats: struggles with long-context consistency; sensitive to temperature >0.7
- Ops notes: quantize to int4 for 2–3x cost reduction, enable KV-prefix caching for conversational workloads.
- Links: repo, license, quick-check report id.

End of note.
